claim: β-Catenin (Ctnnb1) in muscle is critical for motoneuron differentiation.
source: β-Catenin (Ctnnb1) in muscle is critical for motoneuron differentiation; however, little is known about the relevant retrograde signal.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that provides context for the study.

claim: Ctnnb1 mutant without the transactivation domain was unable to rescue presynaptic deficits of Ctnnb1 mutation.
source: We show that Ctnnb1 mutant without the transactivation domain was unable to rescue presynaptic deficits of Ctnnb1 mutation, indicating the involvement of transcription regulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the rescue experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The cell-adhesion function of Ctnnb1 is dispensable for presynaptic differentiation.
source: On the other hand, the cell-adhesion function of Ctnnb1 is dispensable.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the rescue experiments with the TV-AA mutant.

claim: Slit2 was identified as a Ctnnb1-directed retrograde factor.
source: We screened for proteins that may serve as a Ctnnb1-directed retrograde factor and identified Slit2.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the screening experiments.

claim: Transgenic expression of Slit2 specifically in the muscle was able to diminish presynaptic deficits by Ctnnb1 mutation in mice.
source: Transgenic expression of Slit2 specifically in the muscle was able to diminish presynaptic deficits by Ctnnb1 mutation in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the rescue experiments with ACTA1-Slit2 transgenic mice.

claim: Slit2 immobilized on beads was able to induce synaptophysin puncta in axons of spinal cord explants.
source: Slit2 immobilized on beads was able to induce synaptophysin puncta in axons of spinal cord explants.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the synaptogenic assay experiments.

claim: Slit2 serves as a factor utilized by muscle Ctnnb1 to direct presynaptic differentiation.
source: Together, these observations suggest that Slit2 serves as a factor utilized by muscle Ctnnb1 to direct presynaptic differentiation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence in the study.

claim: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is a cholinergic synapse that rapidly conveys signals from motoneurons to muscle cells to control muscle contraction.
source: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is a cholinergic synapse that rapidly conveys signals from motoneurons to muscle cells to control muscle contraction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NMJ.

claim: The NMJ has served as a model to study synaptogenesis.
source: It exhibits a high degree of subcellular specialization characteristic of chemical synapses and has served as a model to study synaptogenesis (Sanes and Lichtman, 2001; Wu et al., 2010; Barik et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Abnormal NMJ formation or function causes neurological disorders including congenital myasthenic syndrome and myasthenia gravis.
source: Abnormal NMJ formation or function causes neurological disorders including congenital myasthenic syndrome and myasthenia gravis.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: NMJ formation requires reciprocal interactions between nerve terminals and muscle cells.
source: NMJ formation requires reciprocal interactions between nerve terminals and muscle cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Nerve-derived agrin directs post-synaptic differentiation by interacting with muscle transmembrane receptors LRP4 and MuSK.
source: In anterograde signaling, nerve-derived agrin directs post-synaptic differentiation by interacting with muscle transmembrane receptors LRP4 and MuSK, which in turn activate downstream signaling events leading to AChR concentration at the NMJ (McMahan, 1990; DeChiara et al., 1996; Glass et al., 1996; Weatherbee et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Much less is known regarding retrograde mechanisms that control motor neuron survival and presynaptic differentiation.
source: However, much less is known regarding retrograde mechanisms that control motor neuron survival and presynaptic differentiation.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Wnt signaling has been implicated in NMJ formation in Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila as well as vertebrates.
source: Wnt signaling has been implicated in NMJ formation in Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila as well as vertebrates (Korkut and Budnik, 2009; Zhang et al., 2009; Barik et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: β-Catenin (Ctnnb1) is a central component of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, regulating transcription by associating with TCF/LEF transcription factors.
source: β-Catenin (Ctnnb1) is a central component of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, regulating transcription by associating with TCF/LEF transcription factors (MacDonald et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ctnnb1 regulates adhesion-dependent signaling by binding to cadherins and α-catenin.
source: It also regulates adhesion-dependent signaling by binding to cadherins and α-catenin (Nelson and Nusse, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: When Ctnnb1 is mutated in muscle fibers, mutant mice die neonatally, with profound presynaptic deficits such as mislocation of phrenic nerve primary branches, reduced synaptic vesicles, and impaired neuromuscular transmission.
source: Intriguingly, when Ctnnb1 is mutated in muscle fibers, mutant mice die neonatally, with profound presynaptic deficits such as mislocation of phrenic nerve primary branches, reduced synaptic vesicles, and impaired neuromuscular transmission (Li et al., 2008), suggesting that Ctnnb1 in muscle cells is necessary for presynaptic differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of stable Ctnnb1 in muscle cells impairs presynaptic differentiation in mutant mice.
source: In support of this notion are recent reports that expression of stable Ctnnb1 in muscle cells also impairs presynaptic differentiation in mutant mice (Liu et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ctnnb1 in muscle is critical for a retrograde pathway to direct nerve terminal development.
source: These observations suggest that Ctnnb1 in muscle is critical for a retrograde pathway to direct nerve terminal development.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies.

claim: The interaction of cadherins of pre- and post-synaptic membranes has been shown to be important for synapse formation.
source: The interaction of cadherins of pre- and post-synaptic membranes has been shown to be important for synapse formation (Bamji et al., 2003; Bozdagi et al., 2004; Prakash et al., 2005) and synaptic plasticity (Murase et al., 2002; Schuman and Murase, 2003; Nuriya and Huganir, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: NMDAR stimulation accumulates Ctnnb1 in spines, which in turn regulates induced endocytosis of N-cadherins.
source: NMDAR stimulation accumulates Ctnnb1 in spines, which in turn regulates induced endocytosis of N-cadherins (Tai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The key amino acid residues in Ctnnb1 for interaction with α-catenin have been mapped to Thr-120 and Val-122.
source: The key amino acid residues in Ctnnb1 for interaction with α-catenin have been mapped to Thr-120 and Val-122 (Aberle et al., 1996a, 1996b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mutation of Thr-120 and Val-122 to alanines prevents Ctnnb1 from binding to α-catenin.
source: Mutation of these two residues to alanines prevents Ctnnb1 from binding to α-catenin (Xu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The TV-AA mutation has no effect on binding to TCF/Lef1, and thus, does not alter the transcription by Ctnnb1 and TCF/Lef1.
source: However, the mutation has no effect on binding to TCF/Lef1, and thus, does not alter the transcription by Ctnnb1 and TCF/Lef1 (Xu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The transcriptional regulation by Ctnnb1 requires the transactivation domain (TAD).
source: On the other hand, the transcriptional regulation requires the transactivation domain (TAD) (Molenaar et al., 1996; van de Wetering et al., 1997; Vleminckx et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ACTA1-Cre::LSL-Ctnnb1, ACTA1-Cre::LSL-Ctnnb1TV-AA, and ACTA1-Cre::LSL-Ctnnb1∆TAD mice were viable and fertile and exhibited normal NMJ morphology, compared to control mice.
source: ACTA1-Cre::LSL-Ctnnb1, ACTA1-Cre::LSL-Ctnnb1TV-AA, and ACTA1-Cre::LSL-Ctnnb1∆TAD mice were viable and fertile and exhibited normal NMJ morphology, compared to control mice (ACTA1-Cre or Ctnnb1fl/fl) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mutants, the primary branches were mislocated to the tendon region close to the central cavity.
source: However, in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− (i.e., CATA1::Cre;Catnnb1f/f) mutants, the primary branches were mislocated to the tendon region close to the central cavity, the secondary branches were fewer and longer, and the region where AChR cluster distributed became wider (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mutants, the secondary branches were fewer and longer.
source: However, in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− (i.e., CATA1::Cre;Catnnb1f/f) mutants, the primary branches were mislocated to the tendon region close to the central cavity, the secondary branches were fewer and longer, and the region where AChR cluster distributed became wider (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mutants, the region where AChR cluster distributed became wider.
source: However, in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− (i.e., CATA1::Cre;Catnnb1f/f) mutants, the primary branches were mislocated to the tendon region close to the central cavity, the secondary branches were fewer and longer, and the region where AChR cluster distributed became wider (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of wild-type Ctnnb1 was able to rescue the presynaptic phenotypes of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: As expected, expression of wild-type Ctnnb1 was able to rescue these phenotypes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The presynaptic phenotypes of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice were completely rescued by Ctnnb1TV-AA.
source: Interestingly, these phenotypes were also completely rescued by Ctnnb1TV-AA since no difference was detectable in primary branch location, secondary branch number and length, and endplate band width between ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1ΔTAD mice and control or ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1 mice, indicating that the cell-adhesion function of Ctnnb1 is not necessary for presynaptic differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The TAD deletion mutant was unable to rescue the presynaptic phenotypes of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: In contrast, however, the TAD deletion mutant was unable to rescue these phenotypes, suggesting a requirement of the transcription function (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The vesicle density in control terminals was 3.6 ± 0.30 vesicles/0.04 μm2.
source: The vesicle density in control terminals was 3.6 ± 0.30 vesicles/0.04 μm2.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data.

claim: The vesicle density was reduced to 1.40 ± 0.37 vesicles/0.04 μm2 in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− terminals.
source: In contrast, the density was reduced to 1.40 ± 0.37 vesicles/0.04 μm2 in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− terminals (p < 0.001), in agreement with previous report (Liu et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data, supported by citations to previous reports.

claim: The reduction in vesicle density in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice was diminished by expressing Ctnnb1 or Ctnnb1TV-AA.
source: As shown in Figure 2, the reduction in vesicle density was diminished by expressing Ctnnb1 or Ctnnb1TV-AA, with 3.6 ± 0.33 and 3.99 ± 0.33 vesicle/0.04 mm2 in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1 mice and ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1TV-AA mice, respectively (p < 0.001 in comparison with ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−, n = 17) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Synaptic vesicle density in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1∆TAD remained low, at 1.33 ± 0.50 vesicles/0.04 μm2.
source: In contrast, synaptic vesicle density in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1∆TAD remained low, at 1.33 ± 0.50 vesicles/0.04 μm2, which was not different from ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice (p > 0.05 in comparison with control; n = 17) (Figure 2A,B), demonstrating inability of the ΔTAD mutant to rescue and suggesting an important role of the transcription regulation in the retrograde pathway.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Active zones were fewer in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice and ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1∆TAD mice, compared with control mice, ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1 mice, and ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1TV-AA mice.
source: Similarly, active zones were fewer in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice and ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1∆TAD mice, compared with control mice, ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1 mice, and ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1TV-AA mice (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Ctnnb1 mutation in muscles did not alter the number of terminals per NMJ and the width of synaptic clefts.
source: As reported previously (Wu et al., 2012a), Ctnnb1 mutation in muscles did not alter the number of terminals per NMJ and the width of synaptic clefts.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of Ctnnb1 wild type or mutants did not change the number of terminals per NMJ and the width of synaptic clefts.
source: Expression of Ctnnb1 wild type or mutants did not change these parameters (Figure 2A,D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Muscle Ctnnb1 mainly regulates presynaptic differentiation.
source: These results are in agreement with the notion that muscle Ctnnb1 mainly regulates presynaptic differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing selective effects on presynaptic parameters.

claim: There was about 50% reduction in mEPP frequency in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice, compared with control mice.
source: There was about 50% reduction in mEPP frequency in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice, compared with control mice (Li et al., 2008) (Figure 3A,B) (1.04 ± 0.04 Hz for control; 0.45 ± 0.04 Hz for ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−, p < 0.001; n = 4), but no change in mEPP amplitude (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3 and a citation to previous work.

claim: There was no change in mEPP amplitude in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: There was about 50% reduction in mEPP frequency in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice, compared with control mice (Li et al., 2008) (Figure 3A,B) (1.04 ± 0.04 Hz for control; 0.45 ± 0.04 Hz for ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−, p < 0.001; n = 4), but no change in mEPP amplitude (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The mEPP frequency reduction phenotype was rescued by both wild-type Ctnnb1 and the TV-AA mutant.
source: The frequency reduction phenotype was rescued by both wild-type Ctnnb1 and the TV-AA mutant (0.95 ± 0.09 Hz in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1 and 1.06 ± 0.04 Hz in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1TV-AA, p > 0.05 in comparison with control; n = 4) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3.

claim: mEPP frequency remained depressed in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1ΔTAD mice.
source: In contrast, mEPP frequency remained depressed in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::LSL-Ctnnb1ΔTAD mice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ctnnb1-regulated transcription is necessary for motor nerve terminal differentiation.
source: Together, these results of both morphological and functional studies indicate the requirement of the Ctnnb1's TAD in motor nerve terminal differentiation and suggest that Ctnnb1-regulated transcription is necessary for motor nerve terminal differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined morphological and functional data.

claim: Ctnnb1 in synaptic nuclei appeared to be higher than that in extra-synaptic regions.
source: First, whole-mount staining of muscle fibers with Ctnnb1 antibody indicates that Ctnnb1 in synaptic nuclei appeared to be higher than that in extra-synaptic regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: β-galactosidase was detectable in synaptic nuclei, not in extra-synaptic nuclei in Axin2-nlacZ mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, β-galactosidase was detectable in synaptic nuclei, not in extra-synaptic nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling is active in synaptic nuclei at the NMJ.
source: These results are in agreement with the notion of active Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling in synaptic nuclei at the NMJ and provide additional support to the model.
evidence: This is inferred from the Axin2-nlacZ reporter data.

claim: C-Myc mRNA was lower in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− muscles than control.
source: C-Myc and Axin2, whose expression is regulated by Ctnnb1 (He et al., 1998; Yan et al., 2001), were used a positive control. Their mRNAs were lower in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− muscles than control, indicating the validity of the method (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Axin2 mRNA was lower in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− muscles than control.
source: C-Myc and Axin2, whose expression is regulated by Ctnnb1 (He et al., 1998; Yan et al., 2001), were used a positive control. Their mRNAs were lower in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− muscles than control, indicating the validity of the method (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Of more than 70 genes screened, 9 were reduced in expression in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−, compared to control Ctnnb1fl/fl mice.
source: In a panel of more than 70 genes, 9 were reduced in expression in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−, compared to control Ctnnb1fl/fl mice (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR screening data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Slit2 is a repulsive axon guidance cue of the Slit family.
source: Of particular interest is Slit2, a repulsive axon guidance cue of the Slit family (Brose et al., 1999; Kidd et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Slit2 as well as Slit1 regulate axon collateral formation.
source: Slit2 as well as Slit1 regulate axon collateral formation (Nguyen Ba-Charvet et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mutation of Slit2, but not Slit1 or Slit3, disrupts motoneuron fasciculation and primary nerve location.
source: Interestingly, mutation of Slit2, but not Slit1 or Slit3, disrupts motoneuron fasciculation and primary nerve location (Jaworski and Tessier-Lavigne, 2012), akin to NMJ morphological deficits of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Of the three members of the Slit family, only Slit2 was down-regulated in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− muscles.
source: Of the three members of the Slit family, only Slit2 was down-regulated in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− muscles (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Slit2 expression was reduced in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− muscle homogenates as confirmed by Western blot analysis.
source: The reduction was also confirmed by Western blot analysis of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− muscle homogenates (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Elevating Ctnnb1 level increased the expression of endogenous Slit2 in C2C12 myotubes in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, elevating Ctnnb1 level increased the expression of endogenous Slit2 in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data from C2C12 cells shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ctnnb1 stimulates the expression of Slit2 in muscle cells.
source: This result indicates that Ctnnb1 stimulates the expression of Slit2 in muscle cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the C2C12 cell data.

claim: Ctnnb1 regulates gene expression by binding to the Tcf4/Lef1 transcription factors.
source: Ctnnb1 regulates gene expression by binding to the Tcf4/Lef1 transcription factors (Behrens et al., 1996; van de Wetering et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: There are putative Tcf4/Lef1-binding sites in the 5′UTR of the Slit2 gene.
source: We identified several putative Tcf4/Lef1-binding sites in the 5′UTR of the Slit2 gene using ChIP-MAPPER (Marinescu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis using ChIP-MAPPER.

claim: There were a Tcf4 and a Lef1 site between −1061 and −929 bases upstream from the transcription initiation site of Slit2.
source: There were a Tcf4 and a Lef1 site between −1061 and −929 bases and two Tcf4 sites between −582 and −567 bases upstream from the transcription initiation site (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There were two Tcf4 sites between −582 and −567 bases upstream from the transcription initiation site of Slit2.
source: There were a Tcf4 and a Lef1 site between −1061 and −929 bases and two Tcf4 sites between −582 and −567 bases upstream from the transcription initiation site (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Ctnnb1 is associated with the Tcf4 sites at −582 to −567 in the Slit2 promoter.
source: As shown in Figure 5E, a specific band was detected using the primers (−582–567), suggesting that Ctnnb1 is associated with the Tcf4 sites.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The Tcf4 and Lef1 sites at −1061 to −929 in the Slit2 promoter may not be able to bind to Ctnnb1.
source: In contrast, no band was detected using the primers (−1061 and −929), although the primers were able to detect a band in input, suggesting that the Tcf4 and Lef1 sites in this region may not be able to bind to Ctnnb1.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ctnnb1 binds to the promoter region of the Slit2 gene to promote its expression in muscle cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that Ctnnb1 binds to the promoter region of the Slit2 gene to promote its expression in muscle cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP and expression data.

claim: The transgene Flag-Slit2 was expressed in muscles of ACTA1-Slit2 mice, but not muscles of control mice.
source: The transgene Flag-Slit2 was expressed in muscles of ACTA1-Slit2 mice, but not muscles of control mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Flag-Slit2 expression was muscle-specific and not detectable in other tissues including the spinal cord.
source: Flag-Slit2 expression was muscle-specific and not detectable in other tissues including the spinal cord (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on data not shown.

claim: Many presynaptic morphological deficits of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice were rescued by Slit2, including reduced nerve terminal coverage.
source: Interestingly, many of presynaptic morphological deficits of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice were rescued by Slit2, including reduced nerve terminal coverage (as indicated by synaptophysin staining) (Figure 6A–C), reduced vesicle density (Figure 7A,B), and reduced active zones (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Reduced vesicle density in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice was rescued by Slit2.
source: Interestingly, many of presynaptic morphological deficits of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice were rescued by Slit2, including reduced nerve terminal coverage (as indicated by synaptophysin staining) (Figure 6A–C), reduced vesicle density (Figure 7A,B), and reduced active zones (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Reduced active zones in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice were rescued by Slit2.
source: Interestingly, many of presynaptic morphological deficits of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice were rescued by Slit2, including reduced nerve terminal coverage (as indicated by synaptophysin staining) (Figure 6A–C), reduced vesicle density (Figure 7A,B), and reduced active zones (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The number of nerve terminals in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mutant or ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::ACTA1-Slit2 rescue mice are not affected.
source: While the number of nerve terminals and synaptic cleft width in either ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mutant or ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::ACTA1-Slit2 rescue mice are not affected (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Synaptic cleft width in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mutant or ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::ACTA1-Slit2 rescue mice are not affected.
source: While the number of nerve terminals and synaptic cleft width in either ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mutant or ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::ACTA1-Slit2 rescue mice are not affected (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Overexpressing Slit2 in muscles was sufficient to diminish presynaptic structural deficits that are caused by muscle Ctnnb1 deficiency.
source: These results indicate that overexpressing Slit2 in muscles was sufficient to diminish presynaptic structural deficits that are caused by muscle Ctnnb1 deficiency, in agreement with the notion that Slit2 acts downstream of Ctnnb1.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue data.

claim: Loss of Ctnnb1 in muscles resulted in reduced mEPP frequency but not amplitude.
source: Loss of Ctnnb1 in muscles resulted in reduced mEPP frequency but not amplitude (Figure 7F–H) (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7 and a citation to previous work.

claim: mEPP frequency in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::ACTA1-Slit2 mice was higher than that of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: Remarkably, mEPP frequency in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/−::ACTA1-Slit2 mice was higher than that of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice, suggesting again that the vesicle release deficit was rescued by muscle expression of Slit2.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Overexpression of Slit2 in muscles had no effect on mislocation of primary nerve branches in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: The rescue effect of nerve terminal structure and function appeared to be specific because overexpression of Slit2 in muscles had no effect on mislocation of primary nerve branches, reduced number of secondary branches, and increased length of secondary branches (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of Slit2 in muscles had no effect on reduced number of secondary branches in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: The rescue effect of nerve terminal structure and function appeared to be specific because overexpression of Slit2 in muscles had no effect on mislocation of primary nerve branches, reduced number of secondary branches, and increased length of secondary branches (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of Slit2 in muscles had no effect on increased length of secondary branches in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: The rescue effect of nerve terminal structure and function appeared to be specific because overexpression of Slit2 in muscles had no effect on mislocation of primary nerve branches, reduced number of secondary branches, and increased length of secondary branches (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ablation of Ctnnb1 in muscles enlarges AChR clusters in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: Ablation of Ctnnb1 in muscles (in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice) enlarges AChR clusters and increased the central band area where AChR clusters are distributed (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Ablation of Ctnnb1 in muscles increased the central band area where AChR clusters are distributed in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: Ablation of Ctnnb1 in muscles (in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice) enlarges AChR clusters and increased the central band area where AChR clusters are distributed (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Slit2 muscle expression had no effect on AChR cluster length of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: Slit2 muscle expression had no effect on AChR cluster length or area of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice (Figure 6A,D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Slit2 muscle expression had no effect on AChR cluster area of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice.
source: Slit2 muscle expression had no effect on AChR cluster length or area of ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice (Figure 6A,D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The enlarged central band area where AChR clusters are distributed in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice was reduced by Slit2 expression.
source: However, the enlarged central band area where AChR clusters are distributed in ACTA1-Ctnnb1−/− mice was reduced (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Muscle-specific expression of Slit2 was able to rescue presynaptic structural and functional deficits at nerve terminals.

claim: In Drosophila, wishful thinking and Glass bottom boat, a TGFβ receptor and ligand, respectively, were shown to be important for presynaptic T-bar formation.
source: In Drosophila, wishful thinking and Glass bottom boat, a TGFβ receptor and ligand, respectively, were shown to be important for presynaptic T-bar formation (Marques et al., 2000; McCabe et al., 2003, 2004).

claim: GDNF was shown to affect pre- and post-synaptic neurotransmission in frog neuron-muscle co-cultures.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Laminin β2 could inhibit neurite outgrowth and regulate nerve terminal differentiation and maturation.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Laminin β2 is thought to bind directly to and cluster calcium channels, which in turn recruit other presynaptic components.

claim: In Integrinβ1 muscle-specific mutant mice, nerve terminal arborization and differentiation are abnormal.

claim: Lrp4 and MuSK were shown to be critical for presynaptic differentiation independently.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Slit2 is a member of the Slit family of secreted glycoproteins, which serve as repulsive cues for axons of various neurons.
source: Slit2 is a member of the Slit family of secreted glycoproteins, which serve as repulsive cues for axons of various neurons (Nguyen-Ba-Charvet et al., 2002; Shu et al., 2003; Marillat et al., 2004; Sabatier et al., 2004; Hussain et al., 2006), as regulators to promote axonal and dendritic branching (Brose et al., 1999; Wang et al., 1999; Nguyen Ba-Charvet et al., 2001; Whitford et al., 2002; Miyashita et al., 2004), and as repellants for neuron migration (Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Slit proteins serve as regulators to promote axonal and dendritic branching.
source: Slit2 is a member of the Slit family of secreted glycoproteins, which serve as repulsive cues for axons of various neurons (Nguyen-Ba-Charvet et al., 2002; Shu et al., 2003; Marillat et al., 2004; Sabatier et al., 2004; Hussain et al., 2006), as regulators to promote axonal and dendritic branching (Brose et al., 1999; Wang et al., 1999; Nguyen Ba-Charvet et al., 2001; Whitford et al., 2002; Miyashita et al., 2004), and as repellants for neuron migration (Wu et al., 1999).

claim: Slit proteins serve as repellants for neuron migration.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Motor neurons use Slit2 to promote their axon fasciculation by an autocrine or juxtaparacrine mechanism.

claim: In Slit2 mutant mice, motor nerves prematurely defasciculate into smaller bundlers in various muscles.
source: In Slit2 mutant mice, motor nerves prematurely defasciculate into smaller bundlers in various muscles, unlike those in wild type that stay in compact fascicle until they reach the middle of muscle fibers.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from previous literature.

claim: NMJ morphology at gross anatomic level appears to be normal in Slit2 mutant mice.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Slit2 is produced by muscle cells in a manner dependent on Ctnnb1.

claim: Slit2, when immobilized on beads, was synaptogenic—to promote the formation and enlargement of synaptophysin-positive puncta.

evidence: This is a primary finding from the synaptogenic assay.

claim: Soluble Slit2 did not have a synaptogenic effect.
source: Soluble Slit2 did not have this effect, suggesting that the effect requires local, high concentration as many synaptogenic proteins do (Dean et al., 2003; Yumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: The synaptogenic effect of Slit2 requires local, high concentration.
source: Soluble Slit2 did not have this effect, suggesting that the effect requires local, high concentration as many synaptogenic proteins do (Dean et al., 2003; Yumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: The high concentration of Slit2 in vivo may be achieved by its enrichment at the NMJ, probably due to the involvement of the laminin-G domain of Slit2's extracellular region.
source: This high concentration in vivo may be achieved by its enrichment at the NMJ, probably due to the involvement of the laminin-G domain of Slit2's extracellular region.

source: The laminin-G domain is known to mediate the SBL immobilization of many proteins including agrin, α-dystroglycan, perlecan, and neurexin (Timpl et al., 2000; Chedotal, 2007).

claim: The LRRs have been conserved in some synaptogenic proteins.
source: The LRRs have been conserved in some synaptogenic proteins (de Wit et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

One includes mislocation of the primary branches of the phrenic nerve and secondary branch arborization and length, while the other consists of synaptic vesicle number reduction, fewer active zones, and reduced mEPP frequency that was due to reduced release probability (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed phenotypes.

claim: The 'trophic' activity of limb buds or muscles identified in the classic limb bud removal experiment is mediated by a Ctnnb1-independent mechanism.
source: This observation suggests that the 'trophic' activity of limb buds or muscles identified in the classic limb bud removal experiment is mediated by a Ctnnb1-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Slit2 does not rescue all deficits.
